citations.quote: Work in $\mathrm{ZF}+\mathrm{AC}$. Let $T=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^r$, $r\ge0$, act continuously on a locally compact Hausdorff space $X$. All vector bundles below have finite complex rank and continuous $T$-linearizations. A **compact-support symbol triple** is $(A,B,s)$, where $A,B\to X$ are such bundles and $s:A\to B$ is an equivariant bundle map that is an isomorphism outside an invariant compact subset of $X$. Isomorphic triples have intertwining bundle isomorphisms. A homotopy of triples is such a triple over $X\times[0,1]$, with trivial action on $[0,1]$, whose noninvertibility set lies in $C\times[0,1]$ for some invariant compact $C\subset X$. A triple is elementary when $s$ is an isomorphism on all of $X$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a finite CW complex. The Chern character
$\operatorname{ch}$ of [[def-chern-character-of-a-complex-vector-bundle]] is
natural for pullbacks, additive over Whitney sums and multiplicative over
tensor products, and it extends uniquely through the Grothendieck completion
to a unital ring homomorphism
$$\operatorname{ch}:K^0(X)\longrightarrow H^{\mathrm{even}}(X;\mathbb Q),$$
whose value on a bundle class is $\operatorname{ch}(E)$. For finite CW
complexes $X,Y$ the external-product formula
$$\operatorname{ch}(a\times b)=\operatorname{ch}(a)\times\operatorname{ch}(b)$$
holds for all $a\in K^0(X)$, $b\in K^0(Y)$, where the external products are
the K-theory and cohomology external products.

Assume AC. For a finite CW pair $(X,A)$ and $j\in\mathbb Z$ write
$$HP^j(X,A;\mathbb Q):=\bigoplus_{k\in\mathbb Z}H^{j+2k}(X,A;\mathbb Q).$$
Negative ordinary cohomology groups are zero. The graded Chern character of
[[def-graded-chern-character-by-suspension-and-bott-periodicity]] extends
naturally to relative groups
$$\operatorname{ch}^j:K^j(X,A)\longrightarrow HP^j(X,A;\mathbb Q),$$
and commutes with the maps and connectors of the pair long exact sequences,
using the ordinary pair-boundary normalization $\partial=-q^*s$
for the cone based at height one as explained below;
in particular
$$\operatorname{ch}^{j+1}\partial_K=\partial_{HP}\operatorname{ch}^j: K^j(A)\longrightarrow HP^{j+1}(X,A;\mathbb Q).$$
For either of these actual theories put
$$F^pE^j(X)=\ker(E^j(X)\longrightarrow E^j(X^{p-1})),$$
where $X^r=\varnothing$ for $r<0$ and $X^r=X$ for $r\ge\dim X$.
Then
$$\operatorname{ch}^j(F^pK^j(X))\subseteq F^pHP^j(X;\mathbb Q).$$
The notation $HP^j$ denotes the displayed periodic sum, not the single
ordinary group $H^j$.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle with $n\geq1$
over a path-connected paracompact Hausdorff CW complex, and let
$q:\operatorname{Fl}(E)\to B$ be its flag bundle, constructed from a Hermitian
metric as in [[def-complex-flag-bundle-and-chern-roots]]. Then
$$q^*E=L_1\oplus L_2\oplus\cdots\oplus L_n$$
with the tautological complex lines $L_i$, and the pullback
$$q^*:H^*(B;R)\longrightarrow H^*(\operatorname{Fl}(E);R)$$
is injective for $R=\mathbb Z$ and for every field $\mathbb F_p$.

Assume AC. For a path-connected CW complex $X$ with a vertex basepoint, the
first Chern class induces a natural group isomorphism
$$c_1:\operatorname{Pic}_{\mathrm{top}}(X)\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }H^2(X;\mathbb Z),$$
where $\operatorname{Pic}_{\mathrm{top}}(X)$ is the group of isomorphism
classes of numerable complex line bundles under tensor product. The same
statement holds for a path-connected paracompact Hausdorff CGWH space of CW
homotopy type.

Assume AC. For every $N\geq0$ identify
$\mathbb{CP}^N=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^{N+1})$, the space of complex
lines in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, and let $\gamma$ be the tautological complex line
with $x=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)$ its Euler class
in the complex orientation. Then, as a graded ring,
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{N+1}),$$
the class $x$ generating each even degree and the odd groups vanishing; for
$0\leq m\leq N$ the standard inclusion
$\mathbb{CP}^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^N$, induced by
$\mathbb C^{m+1}\subseteq\mathbb C^{N+1}$, pulls $x$ back to $x$.

Assume AC.  Every $R$-oriented rank-$n$ numerable vector bundle over a CW
complex, or over a paracompact Hausdorff base of CW type, has a unique
normalized Thom class $u_\xi$, and
$$a\longmapsto\pi^*a\smile u_\xi:H^k(B;R)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R)$$
for every $k$.  Without a supplied orientation, the canonical twisted form is
$$H^k(B;\mathcal O_R(\xi))\xrightarrow{\cong}H^{k+n}(D(\xi),S(\xi);R).$$
The finite supplied-trivializing-cover theorem is a choice-free special case.

Assume AC.  For ordered oriented bundles $\xi\to B$ and $\eta\to C$ of ranks
$n,m$, the canonical product-pair identification gives
$$u_{\xi\times\eta}=u_\xi\times u_\eta.$$
For bundles over one base, diagonal pullback gives
$$u_{\xi\oplus\eta}=u_\xi\smile u_\eta.$$
Interchanging the ordered summands changes the orientation and the displayed
class by the Koszul sign $(-1)^{nm}$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be paracompact Hausdorff and let
$H:X\times I\to Y$ be a homotopy from $f_0$ to $f_1$. For every numerable
finite-rank real or complex vector bundle $E\to Y$, the endpoint pullbacks
$f_0^*E$ and $f_1^*E$ are isomorphic. Equivalently, the restrictions of
$H^*E$ to $X\times\{0\}$ and $X\times\{1\}$ are isomorphic. No canonical
endpoint isomorphism is asserted.

Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring and the orientation is supplied on $M\setminus A$. Its **relative fundamental class** is the unique class
$$[M,A]\in H_n(M,A;R)$$
whose restriction at every interior point is the prescribed local generator. Existence and uniqueness, including manifolds with closed components, are proved in [[lem-a-collar-identifies-boundary-local-homology-with-the-pair-fundamental-class]].

derivations.claim: A compact symbol on a vector bundle over a compact base can be restricted to a closed disk containing its noninvertibility set and radially identified with the disk/sphere pair. Radial contraction of the disk onto its zero section and [F7] identify both bundles there with pullbacks of bundles on the compact base. Its relative K-class is obtained by clutching its two bundles along the sphere using the boundary isomorphism. To see this in the based-quotient model, double the disk, glue the first bundle on its positive half to the second on its negative half, and subtract the doubled second bundle. Add a complement of the second bundle pulled back from the base, so the resulting bundle is trivialized on the negative disk; collapsing that disk gives a reduced virtual bundle on the Thom quotient. Such a complement exists: finitely many local frames and a subordinate partition of unity embed a bundle in a finite trivial bundle, and its orthogonal complement supplies it. Different complements have a common stabilization, and changing the radius or boundary collar gives a homotopy. Conversely, pull a reduced bundle on the quotient back to the positive disk with its boundary trivialization. These operations are inverse after adding elementary triples: the negative half is precisely the trivialized summand removed in the collapse. Thus the ordinary compact triple character used here is [F2]'s relative character, and it respects pullback, extension by zero and products. For products the clutching construction gives tensor products of the resulting reduced virtual bundles; hence [F2]'s ring identity gives the relative product identity.

On $\Lambda^\bullet\mathbb C^r$ put $c(v)=\varepsilon_v-\varepsilon_v^*$ for real $v\in\mathbb C^r$. These are skew-adjoint Clifford matrices; for a unitary basis their two-dimensional factors are exactly the matrices in [F3]'s supplier, and their graded tensors span the full matrix algebra. The action $\Lambda^\bullet u$ of $u\in U(r)$ preserves grading and conjugates $c(v)$ to $c(uv)$. Choose either spin lift $s$ of the realification of $u$. The operator $(\Lambda^\bullet u)\rho(s)^{-1}$ commutes with every Clifford matrix, hence is a unit scalar $z$. Replacing $s$ by $-s$ replaces $z$ by $-z$, so $u\mapsto[s,z]\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(2r)$ is well-defined; local continuous lifts to the spin double cover show continuity, and multiplication of the implementing matrices proves it is a homomorphism. Thus the unitary frame bundle of $W$ induces a specified Spin-c lift whose associated spinor bundle is $\Lambda^\bullet W$. Its Clifford symbol is isomorphic as a relative triple to $D=\varepsilon_v+\varepsilon_v^*$: multiply degree $2j$ in the source by $(-1)^j$ and degree $2j+1$ in the target by $(-1)^j$; exterior multiplication is unchanged and contraction changes sign. In rank zero use the trivial lift and the even line. Therefore [F3] applies to the exact exterior symbol in [F1], with its plane map $z$ and its direct-sum product.

Choose a smooth embedding $f:F\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^N$ and its normal bundle $V$. Such an embedding can be constructed from finitely many coordinate charts and bump functions: take the vector of all functions $\phi_\alpha$ and $\phi_\alpha x_{\alpha,j}$, where the $\phi_\alpha$ are supported inside charts and their positive sets cover $F$. Equality of these vectors determines a common chart with $\phi_\alpha>0$ and then its coordinates, giving injectivity; differentiating the same coordinates shows injectivity of the derivative. Compactness makes it an embedding. An ambient metric splits $f^*T\mathbb R^N=TF\oplus V$ and embeds $T^*F$ into $T^*\mathbb R^N$ by zero normal covector. Its normal bundle, pulled back to $T^*F$, is $V\oplus V^*$: a connection splits horizontal and vertical tangent directions, and the two missing directions are the normal base vector and normal covector. Homotopies of the connection preserve this identification. At the zero section the cotangent symplectic form is the direct sum of the forms on $TF\oplus T^*F$ and $V\oplus V^*$; their symplectic orientations therefore multiply. Fiber dilation contracts $T^*F$ onto its zero section and preserves nondegeneracy, so the same orientation identity holds everywhere.

Let $L$ be a complex line, $x=c_1(L)$, $u_L$ its complex-oriented cohomological Thom class, and $\tau_L$ the plane-normalized Bott symbol [F3]. Thom isomorphism uniquely writes $\operatorname{ch}_c(\tau_L)=u_L A(L)$. The zero-section identity gives $x A(L)=1-e^x$. This equation alone cannot be divided by $x$ on an arbitrary base. Instead apply it to the tautological line on $\mathbb{CP}^k$: for each coefficient through degree $2k-2$, multiplication by $x$ is injective by [F4], so $A(\gamma)=(1-e^x)/x$ through that degree. For any prescribed finite degree choose the stage one degree higher. Compatibility under stage restriction determines every required coefficient, including the constant $-1$. A line on a finite CW base is pulled back from a sufficiently large finite stage of its classifying map, so naturality proves
$$\operatorname{ch}_c(\tau_L)=-u_L e^x\operatorname{Td}(L)^{-1}.$$
This also verifies the sign: on a complex-oriented plane the compact character of the prescribed Bott generator integrates to $-1$.

For a rank-$r$ complex bundle $W$, pull to its flag splitting space. There $W=\bigoplus_jL_j$, and [F3], [F5] and the product identity in step 1.1 give
$$\operatorname{ch}_c(\tau_W)=(-1)^r u_W e^{c_1(W)}\operatorname{Td}(W)^{-1}.$$
Indeed multiplication of the line formulas gives the displayed factor, the sum of the line first Chern classes is $c_1(W)$, and the product of their Todd factors defines the Todd class. To descend, first write the left-hand side as $u_W A(W)$ by the ordinary Thom isomorphism. Pullback preserves $u_W$, and [F4]'s rational injectivity identifies the unique coefficient $A(W)$ with the displayed symmetric series. This proves the formula on the base, including rank zero.

Let $V$ be a real rank-$r$ metric bundle and identify its double $V\oplus V^*$ with $V_{\mathbb C}$ by $(v,\eta)\mapsto v+i\eta^\sharp$. The real structure identifies $V_{\mathbb C}$ with its complex conjugate. Consequently $2c_1(V_{\mathbb C})=0$ and $c_1(V_{\mathbb C})=0$ rationally. The complex orientation is $dv_1\wedge d\eta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dv_r\wedge d\eta_r$, while the cotangent normal orientation is $d\eta_1\wedge dv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d\eta_r\wedge dv_r$; their ratio is $(-1)^r$. If $u_-$ denotes the latter Thom class, step 3.1 therefore becomes
$$\operatorname{ch}_c(\tau_{V_{\mathbb C}})=u_-\operatorname{Td}(V_{\mathbb C})^{-1}.$$
All formulas are invariant under real orthogonal frame changes: their doubled real determinant is positive. Thus they apply without an orientation on $V$ or on its base.

Form $j_!(a)$ by pulling $a$ to that normal bundle, multiplying by $\tau_{V_{\mathbb C}}$, and extending from a tubular neighborhood by zero. A tubular neighborhood exists here directly from the ambient Euclidean normal map: its derivative at the zero section is invertible; the inverse function theorem and compactness of the part of the zero section meeting the support give an injective sufficiently small neighborhood. Shrinking that neighborhood changes its collapse by a radial homotopy. Step 1.1 and step 4.1 give
$$\operatorname{ch}_c(j_!a)=j_*\bigl(\operatorname{ch}_c(a)\,\pi^*\operatorname{Td}(V_{\mathbb C})^{-1}\bigr),$$
where $j_*$ means multiplication by $u_-$ and extension by zero in ordinary compact-support cohomology. For the pairing in [F8], $\int j_*\alpha=\int\alpha$: subdivide a relative fundamental cycle subordinate to normal trivializing neighborhoods, and apply the relative cup-cap pairing on each product disk. The ordered normal Thom generator evaluates to $1$ on its normal disk by normalization, leaving the corresponding tangent coefficient; summing these coefficients gives the original pairing. The local generators of the total fundamental class are exactly these ordered products by step 1.3. Thus this is a cohomological fundamental-class pairing and requires no implicit de Rham comparison. This argument also works for virtual classes and for nonorientable $F$, since its cotangent orientation is global.

By [F3], $K_c^0(T^*\mathbb R^N)$ is the infinite cyclic group generated by the $N$-fold plane Bott product, whose character integrates to $1$ with the $d\theta$ orientation: each factor has complex-oriented integral $-1$ by step 2.1, and reversing each of the $N$ plane orientations supplies another $(-1)^N$. Thus the integer coefficient of $j_!a$ in this generator is its integrated compact character. Since $TF_{\mathbb C}\oplus V_{\mathbb C}$ is trivial, multiplicativity of the Todd series gives $\operatorname{Td}(V_{\mathbb C})^{-1}=\operatorname{Td}(TF_{\mathbb C})$. Integrating step 5.1 proves the first formula for the ordinary class $a$. Its right-hand side uses no embedding or tubular data, so the integer defined by any such construction is independent of those choices.

Put $H=\overline{\langle h\rangle}$ in the acting torus. Since $h$ fixes every point of $F$, continuity makes $H$ act trivially on $F$, hence on $T^*F$. On a compact disk-bundle representative each bundle has only finitely many $H$-weights. Here is a local justification of the finiteness assertion: in a unitary local frame the character is a continuous function of the base point, uniformly on the compact group $H$; its Fourier coefficients are the integer multiplicities of characters. Close base points have uniformly close characters and hence all multiplicities equal, because the coefficient differences have absolute value less than $1$. The weight list is locally constant and the disk has finitely many components. The weight projections are the integrals of the action against the conjugate characters, so are continuous projections of locally constant rank and define eigenbundles. Every equivariant symbol map preserves them. Direct sums, homotopies and elementary triples preserve the resulting weighted ordinary K-class, so $\operatorname{ch}_{h,c}$ is well-defined. Tensoring eigenbundles multiplies eigenvalues, and [F2] gives multiplicativity with an absolute bundle class. Weightwise application of step 6.1 proves the trace-weighted formula. Its degree-zero value on a bundle over a point is $\operatorname{tr}(h)$, whereas the ordinary Chern character's degree-zero value is its dimension; thus a degree-zero Borel rank cannot replace this operation.

On $F\subset M^g$, the fixed subspace of $dg$ is $TF$; the invariant metric gives an orthogonal splitting $TM|_F=TF\oplus
u$ and no $1$-eigenvector in $
u$. The exterior-power identity in [F1] gives the degree-zero term
$$\operatorname{ch}_g(e_g)_{[0]}=\det_{\mathbb C}(I-g|_{
u_{\mathbb C}^*})=\det_{\mathbb R}(I-g|_
u)>0.$$
In the finite-dimensional cohomology ring of $F$, all positive-degree classes are nilpotent. Writing $\operatorname{ch}_g(e_g)=c+u$ with $c$ the nonzero locally constant term, its inverse is the finite geometric sum $c^{-1}\sum_{k\ge0}(-u/c)^k$. Similarly a representation $s$ of nonzero character acts under step 7.1 as the invertible scalar $\chi_s(g)$, so both the weighted character and the weighted pushforward extend by division by this scalar to representation localization. For a localized K-class $b$ with $\pi^*e_g\cdot b=i^*\sigma$, naturality in [F2] and the relative product identity in step 7.1 give $\operatorname{ch}_{g,c}(i^*\sigma)=\pi^*\operatorname{ch}_g(e_g)\,\operatorname{ch}_{g,c}(b)$ on $T^*F$. Pullback preserves the inverse of $\operatorname{ch}_g(e_g)$, so $\operatorname{ch}_{g,c}(b)=\operatorname{ch}_{g,c}(i^*\sigma)/(\pi^*\operatorname{ch}_g(e_g))$. Substitution in step 7.1 proves the second displayed formula whenever the localized quotient exists. In particular it applies to the quotient furnished by a separately proved K-localization theorem; no such theorem was used to prove this comparison.

For an elliptic complex, let $s$ be its symbol differential at a nonzero real covector. Exactness implies that $s+s^*$ has zero kernel: its square is $ss^*+s^*s$, whose quadratic form is $\|su\|^2+\|s^*u\|^2$, and an element killed by both is an element of $\ker s$ orthogonal to $\operatorname{im}s=\ker s$. Thus its even-to-odd block is invertible and defines the same compact-support construction, with no Dirac or isolated-point restriction. A zero-dimensional $F$ has $T^*F=F$, positive point orientations and Todd class $1$, so the integral is the finite fiber trace sum. Finally $(-d\theta)^n=(-1)^n(d\theta)^n$, proving the stated change-of-convention factor. These observations include the empty manifold, zero symbols and rank-zero normals. AC has been used only through the listed topological suppliers and finite smooth bundle constructions.

derivations.claim: Equivariant bundle maps over closed invariant subsets of a compact $T$-space extend to neighborhoods: extend their finitely many local matrix entries with a partition of unity, and average the resulting section of the Hom bundle over $T$. Averaging preserves a map already equivariant on the closed subset. Invertibility is open, so an extended isomorphism is an isomorphism on an invariant neighborhood. Averaging a metric gives invariant orthogonal complements. Applying this extension to successive short subintervals of a homotopy gives equivariant endpoint bundle isomorphisms: identify the bundle with its slice pullback near each slice, subdivide the compact interval, and compose. These arguments also apply relative to a closed invariant subset where the identification is prescribed.

Closed subgroups $H\subset T$ have the following character properties: restriction $\widehat T\to\widehat H$ is onto, and if $g\notin H$ there is $\chi\in\widehat T$ trivial on $H$ with $\chi(g)\ne1$. For completeness, lift $H$ to a closed additive subgroup of $\mathbb R^r$ containing $\mathbb Z^r$. Its vector part and discrete lattice part give, by integer changes of basis and Smith reduction of the lattice relations, coordinates in which $H$ is the product of circle factors, finite cyclic subgroups of circle factors, and identity factors. On a circle factor a character has an arbitrary integer exponent; on a cyclic factor every character is the restriction of an integer exponent modulo its order. This proves surjectivity. In these coordinates failure to belong to $H$ is detected either by a nontrivial coordinate on an identity factor or by the appropriate power on a cyclic factor, proving separation. In particular $R(T)\to R(H)$ is onto, because commuting unitary matrices decompose finite-dimensional representations of compact abelian $H$ into characters.

Every equivariant bundle on a compact $T$-space is an equivariant summand of $Y\times V$ for a finite-dimensional representation $V$. To see this without assuming a nonequivariant complement is equivariant, choose finitely many sections spanning every fiber. With an invariant metric, the action on their Banach space of continuous sections is isometric and continuous. Convolve each section with the product Fejér kernels on $T$. The convolutions converge uniformly: uniform continuity makes translations near the identity uniformly close, and the nonnegative kernels have integral one and mass outside each identity neighborhood tending to zero. Each convolution has only finitely many Fourier characters, so its translates span a finite-dimensional representation. Sufficiently close approximations still span every fiber, since the smallest eigenvalue of the original positive evaluation operator has a positive minimum on compact $Y$. Evaluation from the direct sum of these finite-dimensional section representations is an equivariant surjection; its kernel and invariant orthogonal complement give the assertion.

Apply the invariant-metric exponential chart at a point fixed by $g$. In a sufficiently small invariant ball it intertwines the isometry $g$ with its orthogonal differential, so the fixed points are exactly the exponential of the fixed vector subspace. This proves that $F$ is a closed embedded submanifold, $T_xF=\ker(I-dg_x)$, and its orthogonal normal has no $g$-fixed vector. It is compact and has finitely many components. The cotangent action and the invariant orthogonal splitting imply $X^g=T^*F$. The normal quotient of $T(T^*M)|_{T^*F}$ is canonically an extension of $p^*
u$ by $p^*
u^*$. An invariant connection splits this extension; such a connection is obtained by averaging any metric connection. This gives $p^*(
u\oplus
u^*)$ and the displayed complex structure. Changing the splitting gives a homotopy of these complex normal identifications. The inclusion is proper because it is a closed embedding.

These facts identify triples with reduced equivariant bundle $K$-theory on the one-point compactification. Indeed choose an invariant compact neighborhood of a triple's support; use step 2.1 there to add complements, and use its symbol isomorphism on the surrounding annulus to glue to a constant representation bundle outside. The two resulting bundles agree at infinity. Conversely, a difference of bundles with a chosen isomorphism at infinity extends that isomorphism over a neighborhood by step 1.1 and restricts to a compact-support triple. Refining the neighborhood or complement adds elementary triples, and a changed extension is joined after stabilization by the same annular clutching construction over $[0,1]$. The constructions are inverse because gluing a bundle with its original transition map recovers that bundle. Thus they also identify suspension groups and relative mapping-cone groups, respecting tensor products and extension from open subsets.

Multiplication by $e$ is locally invertible after localization. Fix an orbit in $F$ with stabilizer $H$, so $g\in H$. On its slice $T	imes_H D(V)$ the bundle $
u_{\mathbb C}$ is induced from its fiber representation at the slice center: choose an invariant connection and use radial parallel transport on the slice, which is $H$-equivariant by uniqueness of the parallel-transport equation. This also proves the assertion after shrinking the slice. Thus $e$ there is induced by $\lambda_{-1}(
u_{\mathbb C,x}^*)\in R(H)$. By step 1.2 lift this virtual representation to $s_x\in R(T)$. Its value at $g$ is $\det_{\mathbb C}(I-g|_{

e0$ by step 2.2; hence $s_x\in S_g$. On the slice, multiplication by $e$ equals multiplication by $s_x$, and has inverse $s_x^{-1}$. The same is true over any invariant subset of the slice and on its cotangent preimage under $p$.

For a based compact $T$-space $Y$ and closed invariant based subset $A$, reduced bundle groups are half-exact at $\widetilde K_T^0(Y)$ in the sequence $\widetilde K_T^0(Y\cup_A CA)\to\widetilde K_T^0(Y)\to\widetilde K_T^0(A)$. The composite is zero by the cone contraction. If a bundle difference restricts to zero on $A$, step 2.1 first adds a global complement making its subtracted bundle a constant representation bundle, and then stabilizes the restricted equality to an actual isomorphism with a constant representation bundle on $A$. Glue the positive bundle to that constant bundle on $CA$ by this isomorphism, and subtract the corresponding constant bundle on the whole mapping cone. Their difference extends the original class to $Y\cup_A CA$. This proves the reverse kernel inclusion. Iteratively attach cones; the identifications of two consecutive cone attachments with $SA$ and $SY$ are obtained by collapsing the intervening cone, with the interval coordinates carrying trivial action. The same half-exactness applied after every attachment and every suspension gives the natural long exact sequence extending to all nonpositive degrees. This describes its connecting maps by clutching, rather than postulating them.

Define $j_!$ as follows. Pull back a representative on $T^*F$ to its complex normal $W$, tensor its complex with the Koszul complex of the tautological normal vector, and pass to the even-to-odd map $d+d^*$. In the graded tensor product its square is the sum of the two positive squares, because the two odd summands anticommute; hence its support is contained in the zero section over the original compact support. Compress the normal fibers into a disk tube, and extend to $X$. Extension is the open-extension map established in step 3.1, so this defines a compact-support class even though the Thom symbol alone has noncompact support when $T^*F$ is noncompact. Stable sums, homotopies and elementary classes are respected by tensor product. An isotopy of the tubular map and fiber compression gives a homotopy of compact-support symbols: over a compact base support the normal radii can be bounded uniformly. Restricting the Koszul complex on $\Lambda^ ullet W$ to the zero section sets its differential to zero and leaves $\lambda_{-1}(W)$. The real invariant metric extends to a complex-bilinear equivariant isomorphism $
u_{\mathbb C}\cong
u_{\mathbb C}^*$, so this is precisely $p^*\lambda_{-1}(
u_{\mathbb C}^*)$. Consequently $j^*j_!(b)=p^*\lambda_{-1}(
u_{\mathbb C}^*)b$. This proves self-intersection directly, without invoking an equivariant Thom isomorphism. Suspension gives the same construction in degree one.

The trivial-complex-line Bott isomorphism needed to continue this sequence holds equivariantly. Here is the equivariance check for the explicit ordinary proof [F3]. On $Y\times S^2$ let $T$ act trivially on $S^2$. The hemisphere contractions can be lifted equivariantly by step 1.1, so the clutching automorphism $f(y,z)$ commutes with the fiber action. Laurent coefficients obtained by integration in $z$ therefore intertwine that action. Uniform approximation and the straight-line invertibility homotopy preserve equivariance. Multiplication by powers of $z$, the polynomial linearization block matrices, the Möbius change of the circle variable, and constant frame changes all involve only these equivariant coefficients, scalar functions and identity blocks; hence they are equivariant. The inside and outside generalized eigenspaces are equivariant subbundles, since their polynomial kernels are preserved by every intertwiner. Thus the explicit inverse in [F3] is a map into $K_T^0(Y)\oplus K_T^0(Y)\beta$. Its stabilization, Laurent-shift, direct-sum and homotopy identities hold as equivariant bundle identities by precisely the same matrices; endpoint identifications are equivariant by step 1.1. On $E\boxtimes1$ and $E\boxtimes\beta$ it returns $(E,0)$ and $(0,E)$, respectively. This proves both inverse identities, rather than inferring an equivariant isomorphism merely from an ordinary one. Passing to the kernel of restriction to $Y\vee S^2$ gives product with $\beta$ as an isomorphism for reduced groups; applying the same construction to mapping cones gives the relative version.

Consequently the sequence from step 4.1 continues periodically in both directions. For a closed invariant $A\subset Y$, its relative group equals the compact-support group on $Y\setminus A$: collapse $CA$ in the mapping cone, which does not alter its reduced bundle group. Explicitly a bundle on the contractible cone is a constant representation bundle; extend its chosen trivialization to a neighborhood by step 1.1 and glue to that representation on the collapsed neighborhood. Pullback reverses this operation, including on homotopies. This proves excision. Applied to one-point compactifications and step 3.1, it gives the exact closed/open sequence in both degrees. For an invariant open cover $Y=U\cup V$, compare the closed/open sequences for $(V,V\setminus U)$ and $(Y,Y\setminus U)$, using open extension on $V\to Y$ and $U\cap V\to U$, and the identity on the common closed complement $V\setminus U=Y\setminus U$. A diagram chase yields the cyclic exact sequence $K^q_{T,c}(U\cap V)\to K^q_{T,c}(U)\oplus K^q_{T,c}(V)\to K^q_{T,c}(Y)\to K^{q+1}_{T,c}(U\cap V)$, where the first two maps are the difference of open extensions and their sum. Explicitly lift the image on the common closed complement through either row, subtract its lift in the other row, and use exactness to land in the kernel on the intersection; changing the lift adds exactly the preceding difference map. This proves finite compact-support Mayer–Vietoris. The cone/clutching connecting maps commute with tensoring by a bundle, as do open extension and proper closed restriction. No restriction along a nonproper open inclusion is used. In particular, if both groups vanish on the opens and their intersection, they vanish on the union; if multiplication by a bundle class is invertible on each open and their intersection, the exact sequences give invertibility on the union by lifting and correcting through the adjacent terms.

If $U=T\times_H V$ is a slice neighborhood and $g\notin H$, choose $\chi$ as in step 1.2. The character line over $T/H$ is equivariantly trivial: the function $tH\mapsto\chi(t)$ identifies the ordinary trivial line with its $\chi$ twist. Pullback gives the same identification on $U$ and every invariant subspace of $U$. Thus $1-\chi$ annihilates both compact-support groups of every such subspace, and belongs to $S_g$. All those groups therefore vanish after localization. A compact-support representative on a smooth $T$-manifold having no $g$-fixed points has support covered by finitely many such slices. The slice construction [F2] applies here even when the manifold is noncompact: its exponential proof uses compactness only of the orbit being tubed, and every orbit is compact. Intersections of the finitely many slices are invariant subspaces of a slice. Step 6.1 and induction over this finite cover prove that the representative vanishes after localization. Each class has compact support, so no uniform finite cover of the whole noncompact manifold is required.

The open complement $X\setminus X^g$ has no $g$-fixed points, so both its compact-support groups vanish after localization by step 7.1. Localization preserves exactness: if $u/s$ maps to zero, some $t\in S_g$ kills the image of $u$, and exactness before localization then lifts $tu$, giving a lift of $u/s$ with denominator $ts$. Apply this observation to the exact closed/open sequence of step 6.1 for $(X,X^g)$. The terms on both sides of restriction vanish, proving that $j^*$ is an isomorphism in both degrees.

Compactness of $F$ gives a finite such slice cover. The preimages under $p$ cover $T^*F$, and every intersection lies in a preimage where step 3.2 supplies an inverse. Tensoring with $p^*e$ gives a morphism of the compact-support Mayer–Vietoris sequences. The last assertion of step 6.1, by finite induction, makes it an isomorphism on $S_g^{-1}K^q_{T,c}(T^*F)$. For $a$ set $b=(p^*e)^{-1}j^*a$. Step 4.2 gives $j^*j_!b=j^*a$, and injectivity from step 8.1 gives $j_!b=a$. No claim that the integral Thom map is invertible was needed to derive this localized identity.

The closure of the cyclic group generated by $g$ acts trivially on $F$. On each fiber it is a commuting family of unitary transformations. Character averaging gives its eigenspace projections as smooth bundle endomorphisms. Their ranks are locally constant; near each base point the finitely many projections already spanning the fiber exhaust its rank, so no new character occurs nearby. Compactness therefore gives finitely many eigenbundles globally. The same projections on bundles over $T^*F$ preserve symbols and compact support. Taking the weighted sum of these bundles is additive and multiplicative under tensor product, because eigenvalues multiply; on the scalar action of $s\in R(T)$ it multiplies by $s(g)$. This proves the asserted extension of $\operatorname{tr}_g$ to localized groups and its compatibility with the reconstruction identity. Expanding exterior powers of a direct sum proves the displayed formula for $\operatorname{tr}_g(e)$. Fiberwise its rank is the product of $1-\zeta$ over the eigenvalues of $g$ on $\nu_{\mathbb C}^*$, hence the displayed determinant. Orthogonality identifies the dual eigenvalue multiset with the original one, and complexification preserves the real characteristic polynomial, giving equality with the real determinant.

The proof applies to every triple and its suspension, without any restriction on its origin. The normal bundle has rank zero when $F=M$, in which case $e=1$ and $j$ is the identity; when $F$ is empty step 7.1 gives zero localized groups. For an isolated fixed point $K^0(F)=\mathbb Z$, so the character denominator is its scalar determinant. For a component of positive dimension the preceding proof retains all its exterior-power bundle classes. This completes all the assertions.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to a representative of a compact-support triple. Its continuous bundles and maps are smoothed, radially identified with base bundles, and represented by a homogeneous elliptic symbol by the proved constructions in that supplier. Every relation in the group of [F1] is preserved by [F2], so its additive index descends to $a_{T,M}$. Tensoring by representations proves $R(T)$-linearity. The same supplier proves the claimed operator and complex identifications, using matrix ellipticity and harmonic representatives. Its group restriction and diffeomorphism assertions give the stated naturality. In particular this step constructs an index on symbols; it does not assume an embedding theorem for that index.

First consider the zero section of a real rank-$k$ equivariant metric bundle $N\to Y$. Its orthonormal frame bundle $P\to Y$ is a smooth principal right $O(k)$-bundle; $T$ acts on frames by the differential fiber action and commutes with right multiplication. Its compact normal sphere bundle is $Z=P\times_{O(k)}S(\mathbb R^k\oplus\mathbb R)$. It has an invariant open chart $P\times_{O(k)}\mathbb R^k=N$ around its north section. The vertical compact symbol is the $O(k)$-equivariant extension of $b_{\mathbb R^k}$ from this chart. By [F2] it has a smooth equivariant homogeneous realization, whose order may be changed to one without changing its class or index. Its finite-dimensional kernel $K$ and adjoint kernel $L$ obey $[K]-[L]=1$ by [F4]. Invariant orthogonal decompositions into irreducible finite-dimensional $O(k)$ modules then give an actual $O(k)$-equivariant isomorphism $K\cong L\oplus\mathbb C$: equality of their multiplicities is exactly this virtual equality. The fiber has trivial additional $T$ action, so the associated isomorphism is also $T$-equivariant.

Represent $c$ by an order-one elliptic symbol on $Y$ using [F2], and apply [F3] to this base symbol and the vertical sphere symbol of step 1.2. The product index is the difference of the indices twisted by $K_P$ and $L_P$. Their equivariant bundle isomorphism $K_P\cong L_P\oplus\mathbb C_Y$, block additivity and quantization independence in [F2] make that difference exactly $a_{T,Y}(c)$. This statement concerns all symbol classes: a virtual difference of representatives is handled additively, and no differential or Dirac representative is required.

In a frame chart of $N$, split a covector on its total space into $(\alpha;v,\eta)$, with $\alpha\in T^*Y$ and $(v,\eta)$ the normal base and normal covector. The restriction of the associated product class from step 2.1 to $T^*N$ is the graded product of $c(\alpha)$ and the normal Koszul map at $v+i\eta^\sharp$. Its possible noninvertibility is the zero normal vector/covector over the compact support of $c$. The tensor differential contracts wherever either factor is invertible, so it has compact support. These local maps patch because real orthogonal frame changes intertwine exterior multiplication and its adjoint. A connection gives the indicated cotangent splitting; varying it is an affine homotopy, and [F3] proves the corresponding elliptic product-symbol homotopy. This is exactly the doubled-normal symbol defining the zero-section $j_!$ in [F1]. Thus the associated product is its extension from the normal open chart, rather than an unrelated symbol of the same dimension.

For $f:Y\hookrightarrow M$, use [F5] to identify a disk neighborhood in $N$ equivariantly with a neighborhood of $Y$ in $M$. Fiber compression identifies the compact symbol in step 3.1 with one supported in this disk tube: over the compact support of $c$, choose one uniformly small normal radius, and compress the normal coordinates by a radial diffeomorphism. The same invariant open disk tube embeds in the compact sphere bundle $Z$ and in $M$. Its cotangent identifications have precisely normal complex structure $J(v,\eta)=(-\eta^\sharp,v^\flat)$; the differential of the tube map gives this along the zero section, and the connection splittings are joined by the homotopy just used. The controlled two-cutoff excision in [F2] identifies the kernel and adjoint-kernel representations of the extensions into $Z$ and $M$. Combining this equality with step 2.1 proves $a_{T,M}(j_!c)=a_{T,Y}(c)$. Normal ranks constant only componentwise cause no difficulty: compactness gives finitely many components, and apply the argument to each and add. For rank zero the tube is an open-and-closed component and the assertion is direct extension by zero; empty manifolds give zero.

For the trivial group, construct an embedding $Y\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^N$ by finitely many chart functions: choose bump functions $\phi_i$ supported in coordinate charts whose positive sets cover $Y$, and map to the vector of all $\phi_i$ and $\phi_i x_{i,j}$. Equality determines a common positive chart and then its coordinates, proving injectivity; the same coordinate ratios show that the derivative is injective. Compactness makes it an embedding. Regard its target as the open Euclidean chart of $S^N$. Step 4.1 identifies the analytic index of $Y$ with the index of its doubled-normal extension to that sphere, and [F2] computes the latter in the Euclidean chart. By [F6], its class there is the integer $p_{Y,!}(c)$ times $b_{\mathbb R^N}$. The normalization [F4], restricted to the trivial group, sends this generator to $1$. Hence $a_{\{1\},Y}(c)=p_{Y,!}(c)$. The left-hand side is intrinsic, proving the asserted independence of embedding. This uses only ordinary Bott periodicity; no equivariant representation Bott isomorphism has been presumed.

Suppose $g$ fixes $Y$ pointwise. The compact closure $H=\overline{\langle g\rangle}$ then fixes $Y$ and its cotangent bundle. On a compact disk representative, its unitary bundle representations have finitely many weights: character integration gives continuous projection operators onto each weight, whose ranks are locally constant. The finitely many weights spanning a fiber still exhaust its rank on a neighborhood; compactness gives a finite global list. Their projections split the bundles and preserve the symbol. Quantize the finite blocks separately and average over $H$. The resulting elliptic operator represents the restricted symbol, and its kernel and adjoint kernel split into the same weight blocks. Consequently its character at $g$ is $\sum_\lambda\lambda a_{\{1\},Y}(c_\lambda)$; quantization independence and group restriction in [F2] identify it with the character of $a_{T,Y}(c)$. Step 5.1 gives the stated formula with $p_{Y,!}$. Finally every index identity is $R(T)$-linear, and evaluation of $s\in R(T)$ at $g$ is a scalar. Localizing where $s(g)\ne0$ therefore extends the identities by ordinary division, proving the last assertion.
